summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a public web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx observations into an accessible time-lapse of any patch of sky. Users can search by object name or Right Ascension/Declination, choose a field of view, detector band, and data release, then play up to eight real observation frames in chronological order. Our FastAPI backend queries the live IRSA archive, retrieves compact FITS cutouts instead of massive source files, converts calibrated image data into viewable PNGs, and caches results for faster repeat exploration. The viewer includes shared search links, guided challenge targets, detector/wavelength context, and reference sky imagery.

By making “blink comparison” simple and visual, SPHEREx Blink helps citizen scientists distinguish objects that move across the sky from objects whose brightness changes. It lowers the barrier to exploring a rapidly growing infrared survey and invites more people to participate in finding new brown dwarfs, asteroids, comets, and variable objects.
details:
SPHEREx Blink

See the sky change. Help discover what is hidden in plain sight.

SPHEREx Blink is a public-facing web application that turns NASA SPHEREx near-infrared observations into an intuitive, interactive “blink” viewer. It lets anyone compare the same patch of sky across time and identify objects that move or change in brightness—the same visual method that has helped astronomers and citizen scientists discover asteroids, comets, nearby stars, and brown dwarfs.

What we developed

We built a complete web-to-archive discovery workflow:

  1. A user searches by object name or Right Ascension / Declination in decimal degrees or sexagesimal notation.
  2. They select a field of view, one of SPHEREx’s six detectors (D1–D6), and a data release.
  3. Our backend queries the live NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) for SPHEREx observations covering that position.
  4. It requests efficient FITS cutouts rather than downloading full spectral-image files, converts calibrated image data into viewable PNGs, and returns chronological metadata.
  5. The frontend presents up to eight frames in an interactive player, making motion and flux changes easy to inspect visually.

Search by name or coordinates
↓
IRSA SPHEREx archive query
↓
FITS cutouts + calibrated IMAGE extension
↓
Image stretch and PNG conversion
↓
Chronological blink player for discovery

Why it addresses the challenge

SPHEREx is producing an extraordinary all-sky infrared record, but its scale makes manual inspection difficult. SPHEREx Blink lowers that barrier. Instead of asking users to understand FITS files, infrared calibration, or archive protocols before they can participate, the project turns the essential discovery task into a clear visual question:

Did this object change position, or did its brightness change?

The tool supports the challenge’s required examples:

  • Barnard’s Star: a nearby, high-proper-motion star.
  • WISE 0855: a faint, cold, fast-moving brown dwarf.
  • Epsilon Indi B: brown dwarfs near a bright star.
  • RW Aurigae and R Draconis: variable stars whose brightness changes rather than their position.

It also includes additional coordinate-backed targets, a searchable target catalogue, shareable URLs, and an “own coordinates” path so exploration is not limited to presets.


Key features

Interactive time-domain viewer

  • Play, pause, previous/next-frame controls, playback-speed selection, and a timeline slider.
  • Observation time, detector, wavelength range, and frame number displayed for each image.
  • Frames sorted oldest first for scientifically meaningful comparisons.
  • Clear loading, no-coverage, fallback, failed-image, and upstream-error states.

SPHEREx-aware search

  • Coordinates accept decimal degrees or astronomy-standard sexagesimal notation.
  • Name lookup and coordinate priority support both beginners and advanced users.
  • Field of view is adjustable from a focused patch to a wider context, up to 0.5°.
  • Detector selection exposes the mission’s wavelength coverage from 0.75–5.00 μm.
  • Automatic QR3 → QR2 fallback helps users find available data; WISE 0855 is preconfigured for QR2 coverage.

Reference context and education

  • A responsive reference sky panel provides visual context without presenting non-SPHEREx imagery as mission data.
  • A dedicated About experience explains SPHEREx, its six detectors, wavelength ranges, and the difference between motion and variability.
  • The interface reminds users to compare frames from the same detector and similar wavelengths—an essential safeguard against false visual changes.

Built for sharing and public participation

  • Searches are encoded in the URL, allowing discoveries, target configurations, and demonstrations to be shared directly.
  • Curated challenge targets are prominently separated from additional exploration targets.
  • The responsive interface works across desktop and phone layouts, with reduced-motion support for accessibility.

What makes it technically and creatively different

The creative core of SPHEREx Blink is translating a professional astronomy workflow into a beautiful, understandable public instrument. We combine an immersive celestial interface with careful data handling: no synthetic observations are generated, and the viewer distinguishes mission frames from reference imagery.

The FastAPI backend uses Astropy, astroquery, and the IRSA SIA interface to locate observations; it validates coordinates, filters by detector, samples epochs, retrieves cutouts concurrently, caches search results and rendered frames, and converts the calibrated FITS IMAGE extension using percentile/asinh stretching. This makes the images legible while preserving a realistic path from archive product to viewer.

The Next.js frontend is designed as a discovery experience rather than a raw data portal. It combines a HeroUI-powered search workflow with fluid transitions, curated targets, explanatory context, and responsive visual feedback so that first-time users can begin exploring quickly.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, HeroUI, Framer Motion, and React Bits.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, and httpx.
  • Astronomy and image processing: Astropy, astroquery, NumPy, Pillow, and FITS.
  • Data source: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) and SPHEREx Quick Release products.
  • Deployment architecture: A server-side API proxy, cached image products, and an environment-configured backend origin.

Intended impact

SPHEREx Blink makes a growing infrared sky archive feel explorable rather than overwhelming. Its goal is to help students, educators, amateur astronomers, and citizen scientists take part in the first stage of discovery: noticing what changed.

By combining live archive access with a simple blink interface, the project can help broaden participation in searches for moving nearby objects, brown dwarfs, variable stars, and potentially unexpected transient phenomena. It also gives users an intuitive entry point into infrared astronomy and the scientific value of repeated observations over time.
